date: 2026-09-09
categories: [tool, geoml, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre — upload a point file (or use the built-in example), run DBSCAN, see how a distance in meters requires picking a real coordinate system first, and why the two languages label the exact same groups with different numbers."
---

Some questions aren't "is this one point inside that polygon" — they're
"which of these points belong together, and which don't belong
anywhere." DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications
with Noise) answers that by density: a point belongs to a cluster if
enough other points sit close enough to it — no need to decide the
number of clusters in advance, and no need to force every point into
a group. A point too far from everything else stays *noise*, not a
cluster of one.

A `.geojson`, or a shapefile (either as a single `.zip`, or as
`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together) — see the upload section
below.

Just want to cluster a file with adjustable settings and a download
button, without the rest of the reading? Use the
[standalone tool](/tools/spatial-clustering-explorer.html) — same
engine, less prose.

## 1. Why the coordinate system matters here

DBSCAN takes one distance, ε (`eps`): how close two points need to be
to count as neighbors. For that distance to mean anything, it has to
be in real units — meters — not degrees of longitude/latitude, where
the same number of degrees covers very different real distances
depending on where on Earth you are. Both languages below pick a
working UTM zone from the data's own bounding-box center and
reproject into it first — same reasoning, same formula, as this
site's [Viewshed](raster-viewshed.qmd) tool: a reasonable default for
one local dataset, not a universally correct choice for points
spanning multiple UTM zones or very large areas.

built-in example: two tight groups of six points, and two points far

on *how the two languages report a result*, not on tuning — the
[standalone tool](/tools/spatial-clustering-explorer.html) exposes
both as adjustable controls.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-clustering-py}
#| package: geopandas, scikit-learn
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

# Same 14-point layout as the article's original fixed dataset -- used
# only when nothing was uploaded, so the point-by-point table in
# section 4 stays readable by default.
FALLBACK_LONS = [12.4500, 12.4503, 12.4498, 12.4501, 12.4499, 12.4502,
                  12.4700, 12.4703, 12.4698, 12.4701, 12.4699, 12.4702,
                  12.4300, 12.5000]
FALLBACK_LATS = [41.9000, 41.9002, 41.8998, 41.9001, 41.8999, 41.9003,
                  41.9050, 41.9052, 41.9048, 41.9051, 41.9049, 41.9053,
                  41.8800, 41.9300]

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
if gdf is None:
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(FALLBACK_LONS, FALLBACK_LATS), crs="EPSG:4326")
else:
    if gdf.crs is None:
        gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
        crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
    elif str(gdf.crs) != "EPSG:4326":
        gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone

# Centroid computed AFTER reprojecting into a projected CRS on
# purpose -- the same call on the geographic gdf above would trigger a
# real GeoPandas warning ("Results from 'centroid' are likely
# incorrect"), same reasoning as this site's Spatial Clustering
# Explorer tool.
gdf_proj = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
coords = np.column_stack([gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.x, gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.y])

# A single UTM zone distorts badly -- to the point of returning inf --
# for points far enough from it (a real crash a global file can
# trigger, found and fixed in the standalone Spatial Clustering
# Explorer tool). The tool degrades by dropping those points; this
# article fails loudly instead, on purpose -- section 4 below compares
# Python's and R's labels BY POSITION, point for point, so silently
# dropping a different subset in each language would desync that
# comparison rather than just shrink it.
if not np.isfinite(coords).all():
    raise ValueError(
        f"This file spans too wide an area to project into a single UTM "
        f"zone ({calc_epsg}) -- some points map to infinity. Try a smaller, "
        "more local file, or use the standalone tool, which handles this by "
        "excluding the unprojectable points instead of failing."
    )

# scikit-learn's own convention: noise is -1, real clusters start at 0.
labels = DBSCAN(eps=100, min_samples=4).fit(coords).labels_
gdf["cluster"] = [int(l) for l in labels]

{
    "features": gdf.__geo_interface__,
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "labels": [int(l) for l in labels],
    "uniqueLabels": sorted(int(l) for l in set(labels)),
    "noiseCount": int((labels == -1).sum()),
    "crsWarning": crs_warning
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-clustering-r}
#| package: dbscan, sf, jsonlite
library(dbscan)
library(sf)

FALLBACK_LONS <- c(12.4500, 12.4503, 12.4498, 12.4501, 12.4499, 12.4502,
                    12.4700, 12.4703, 12.4698, 12.4701, 12.4699, 12.4702,
                    12.4300, 12.5000)
FALLBACK_LATS <- c(41.9000, 41.9002, 41.8998, 41.9001, 41.8999, 41.9003,
                    41.9050, 41.9052, 41.9048, 41.9051, 41.9049, 41.9053,
                    41.8800, 41.9300)

data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (is.null(data)) {
  data <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lon = FALLBACK_LONS, lat = FALLBACK_LATS), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
} else if (is.na(st_crs(data))) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!isTRUE(st_crs(data) == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
bnd <- st_bbox(data)
center_lon <- (bnd[["xmin"]] + bnd[["xmax"]]) / 2
center_lat <- (bnd[["ymin"]] + bnd[["ymax"]]) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone

data_proj <- st_transform(data, calc_epsg)
coords_calc <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(data_proj)))

# Same reasoning as the Python cell's own check above: a single UTM
# zone can map far-away points to infinity, and this article fails
# loudly rather than dropping points, to keep the by-position label
# comparison in section 4 meaningful.
if (!all(is.finite(coords_calc))) {
  stop(paste0(
    "This file spans too wide an area to project into a single UTM zone (",
    calc_epsg, ") -- some points map to infinity. Try a smaller, more ",
    "local file, or use the standalone tool, which handles this by ",
    "excluding the unprojectable points instead of failing."
  ))
}

# dbscan's own convention: noise is 0, real clusters start at 1 -- a
# real point of divergence from scikit-learn, not a formatting detail.
# See section 4 below.
res <- dbscan(coords_calc, eps = 100, minPts = 4)

result <- list(
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  labels = as.integer(res$cluster),
  uniqueLabels = sort(unique(as.integer(res$cluster))),
  noiseCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(sum(res$cluster == 0))),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning)
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Warm-palette hues from _brand.yml, same palette/roles as the
// Spatial Clustering Explorer tool -- reused here rather than
// invented fresh, so a reader who's seen the tool recognizes the
// same visual language.
CLUSTER_PALETTE = ["#ab502b", "#42583c", "#3d5a73", "#c48a2e", "#8b2f24"]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
NOISE_COLOR = "#766851"
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// The map shows Python's own partition/coloring only -- not because
// R's result is somehow secondary, but because both languages agree
// on WHICH points group together (that's the whole point of section
// 4 below); drawing the same partition twice, in two different label
// numberings, would just be two circle layers stacked on identical
// coordinates with one hiding the other.
clusterPaint = (clusterIds) => {
  // Same real edge case handled in the standalone tool: sparse data at
  // fixed ε/min points can come back as all noise, zero real clusters
  // -- an empty clusterIds would build an invalid MapLibre "match"
  // expression (it needs at least one pair before its fallback).
  if (clusterIds.length === 0) {
    return {
      "circle-color": NOISE_COLOR,
      "circle-radius": 6,
      "circle-stroke-width": 1,
      "circle-stroke-color": "#2a2117"
    };
  }
  const expr = ["match", ["get", "cluster"]];
  clusterIds.forEach((id, i) => {
    expr.push(id, CLUSTER_PALETTE[i % CLUSTER_PALETTE.length]);
  });
  expr.push(NOISE_COLOR);
  return {
    "circle-color": expr,
    "circle-radius": 6,
    "circle-stroke-width": 1,
    "circle-stroke-color": "#2a2117"
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = rowLabel;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };

  if (!s) {
    row("Calculation CRS", "—");
    return wrap;
  }

  row("Calculation CRS", s.calculationCrs);
  row("Labels used", s.uniqueLabels.join(", "));
  row("Noise points", s.noiseCount);

  return wrap;
}
```

## 4. A label is not a name

Both cards above found the same thing: two groups of six, and two
noise points (with the built-in example — an upload of your own may
find something different). But the *numbers* don't match — and that's
not a bug in either language.

Two separate reasons, easy to conflate:

- **DBSCAN's own cluster numbering is arbitrary.** Nothing about
  "cluster 0" or "cluster 1" is meaningful on its own — it's just the
  order the algorithm happened to visit points in. Run the same
  algorithm again with the points in a different order (or on a
  different implementation entirely) and the *groupings* can come out
  identical while the *numbers* attached to them differ.
- **scikit-learn and `dbscan` also disagree on noise, specifically.**
  This one isn't arbitrary — it's a real, documented difference
  between the two libraries: scikit-learn labels noise `-1` and starts
  real clusters at `0`; R's `dbscan` package labels noise `0` and
  starts real clusters at `1`. Every non-noise label is shifted by
  exactly one.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
labelTable = {
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  if (!pySummary || !rSummary) {
    wrap.textContent = "Run both cells above to compare.";
    return wrap;
  }
  const table = document.createElement("table");
  table.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  table.style.display = "table";
  table.style.width = "100%";

  const headRow = document.createElement("tr");
  ["Point #", "Python label", "R label"].forEach((h) => {
    const th = document.createElement("th");
    th.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    th.textContent = h;
    headRow.appendChild(th);
  });
  table.appendChild(headRow);

  pySummary.labels.forEach((pyLabel, i) => {
    const tr = document.createElement("tr");
    [String(i + 1), String(pyLabel), String(rSummary.labels[i])].forEach((text) => {
      const td = document.createElement("td");
      td.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
      td.textContent = text;
      tr.appendChild(td);
    });
    table.appendChild(tr);
  });

  wrap.appendChild(table);
  return wrap;
}
```

${labelTable}

Read down the table: every point Python calls `0`, R calls `1`; every
point Python calls `1`, R calls `2`; every point Python calls `-1`
(noise), R calls `0`. The *partition* — which points end up
together — is identical. The *labels* attached to it aren't, and
never had to be.

::: {.callout-note}
This is why comparing two clustering results — across languages, or
across two runs of the same algorithm — should compare **who's grouped
with whom**, never raw label equality. In practice: pick any two
points, and ask "does language A say they're in the same group, and
does language B agree?" — repeat for every pair, and you're comparing
partitions, not numbers that were never meant to match.
:::

## 5. Where to next

- **Just needed to cluster a file, with adjustable settings and a
  download button?** → The
  [standalone Spatial Clustering Explorer](/tools/spatial-clustering-explorer.html)
  runs the same detection on an uploaded point file (or its own
  example), with adjustable ε and minimum group size, colored on the
  map, downloadable.
- **Wondering why the coordinate system needed picking at all?** →
  [Coordinate Reference Systems](crs-mismatch.qmd) covers the
  geographic/projected distinction this article leaned on in section 1.
- **Have labels already, and want to predict them somewhere new
  instead of finding groups from scratch?** →
  [Predicting Spatial Classes with Random Forest](spatial-classification.qmd)
  is this family's supervised counterpart to DBSCAN.
